clinicalPearls: Autosomal recessive juvenile or young-adult-onset parkinsonism caused by ATP13A2 (PARK9) variants, first described in a consanguineous family from the Kufor-Rakeb region of Jordan.
The signature is levodopa-responsive parkinsonism combined with pyramidal (spastic) signs, marking it as an atypical parkinsonism rather than classic young-onset Parkinson disease.
Supranuclear vertical gaze palsy with slow saccades is characteristic.
Facial-faucial-finger mini-myoclonus (fine myoclonic twitching) is a distinctive sign; oculogyric dystonic spasms and visual hallucinations also occur.
Despite a good initial response, levodopa-induced dyskinesias and motor fluctuations tend to appear early.
Progressive cognitive decline leading to dementia, together with psychiatric symptoms, is typical.
ATP13A2 encodes a lysosomal P5-type transport ATPase, so this is fundamentally a lysosomal storage/handling disorder; allelic variants also cause a form of neuronal ceroid lipofuscinosis.
MRI often shows diffuse cerebral and cerebellar atrophy, and basal ganglia iron accumulation may be seen, placing the syndrome within the NBIA spectrum.
reference.pathophysiology: ATP13A2, on chromosome 1p36, encodes a lysosomal type 5 P-type transport ATPase that handles cations such as zinc and manganese and transports polyamines, supporting lysosomal acidification and the autophagy-lysosome degradation pathway. Loss-of-function variants impair lysosomal proteolysis and autophagic clearance, so that alpha-synuclein and other substrates accumulate, mitochondrial function is compromised, and cellular handling of divalent metals (manganese, zinc and iron) becomes dysregulated. The resulting neuronal loss is prominent in the substantia nigra, producing levodopa-responsive parkinsonism, but extends widely to cause pyramidal signs, supranuclear gaze impairment, myoclonus and dementia. The overlap of lysosomal dysfunction with iron dyshomeostasis explains why the disorder sits at the intersection of the parkinsonism, NBIA and neuronal ceroid lipofuscinosis spectra, and inheritance is autosomal recessive, often in consanguineous families.
additionalDifferentials: Niemann-Pick disease type C (young-onset extrapyramidal features with vertical gaze palsy)
Progressive supranuclear palsy (for the gaze palsy)
additionalInvestigations: Brain MRI with iron-sensitive sequences and volumetric assessment to demonstrate atrophy and basal ganglia iron
ATP13A2 testing within a parkinsonism/NBIA gene panel
Serum caeruloplasmin, copper studies and slit-lamp examination for Kayser-Fleischer rings to exclude Wilson disease
Dopamine transporter (DAT) imaging showing a presynaptic dopaminergic deficit
Oculomotor assessment for supranuclear gaze palsy and saccadic slowing
Specialist metabolic testing to exclude Niemann-Pick disease type C, and neuropsychological assessment
redFlags: Rapid cognitive and motor deterioration in a young person with parkinsonism
Recurrent falls from combined parkinsonism, spasticity and gaze palsy
reference.prognosis: The syndrome is progressive, with severe combined disability from parkinsonism, spasticity and dementia typically developing within roughly a decade of onset. Levodopa helps early on, but treatment is limited by early dyskinesias.
pitfalls: Labelling it as ordinary young-onset Parkinson disease and missing the pyramidal signs, supranuclear gaze palsy and mini-myoclonus that mark an atypical parkinsonism.
Failing to exclude Wilson disease and Niemann-Pick type C, which share young-onset extrapyramidal features and vertical gaze abnormalities.
Overlooking the lysosomal/NBIA and neuronal ceroid lipofuscinosis overlap and its implications for targeted testing.
Attributing the early dyskinesias to overtreatment rather than to the underlying disorder.
